t: Which of the following represents the correct order of stability of the given carbocations?
s:
The stability of a carbocation is inversely proportional to the strength of the electron-withdrawing groups attached to it due to the -I (inductive) effect. Electron-withdrawing groups pull electron density away from the positively charged carbon, intensifying the positive charge and destabilizing the carbocation.
In H₃C⁺, there are no strong electron-withdrawing groups, making it the most stable among the given species.
In F₃C−CH₂⁺, the highly electronegative −CF₃ group exerts a strong -I effect on the adjacent positively charged carbon, destabilizing the system.
In F₃C⁺, three highly electronegative fluorine atoms are directly attached to the positively charged carbon. The inductive effect is distance-dependent and is significantly stronger when the electron-withdrawing atoms are directly bonded to the charged center. Consequently, the destabilizing -I effect in F₃C⁺ is much stronger than in F₃C−CH₂⁺, rendering F₃C⁺ the least stable.
Therefore, the correct order of stability is H₃C⁺>F₃C−CH₂⁺>F₃C⁺.

t: Arrange the following free radicals in the correct order of their stability (i) CH₂=C^(•)H (ii) C^(•)H₃ (iii) CH₃−C^(•)H−CH₃ (iv) (CH₃)₃Ċ
s:
The stability of alkyl free radicals is determined by hyperconjugation and the inductive effect (+I). The greater the number of α-hydrogen atoms, the more stable the free radical.
The radical in (iv), (CH₃)₃C^•, is a tertiary (3°) free radical. It has 9 α-hydrogen atoms, leading to maximum hyperconjugation. Thus, it is the most stable.
The radical in (iii), CH₃−C^•H−CH₃, is a secondary (2°) free radical with 6 α-hydrogen atoms. It is less stable than a tertiary radical but more stable than a methyl radical.
The radical in (ii), C^•H₃, is a methyl free radical. It has no α-hydrogen atoms and no stabilization through hyperconjugation, making it less stable than secondary and tertiary radicals.
The radical in (i), CH₂=C^•H, is a vinyl free radical. The unpaired electron resides in an sp² hybridized orbital. Due to the higher s-character of the sp² orbital compared to the pure p-orbital containing the unpaired electron in alkyl radicals, the electron is held closer to the electronegative nucleus. This lack of delocalization and strong nuclear attraction makes the vinyl radical the least stable of the given options.
Therefore, the correct decreasing order of stability is (iv) > (iii) > (ii) > (i).

t: All the hydrocarbons shown are very weak acids. One, however, is far more acidic than the others. Which one is the strongest acid?
s:
The acidity of a hydrocarbon is determined by the stability of its conjugate base. A more stable conjugate base implies a stronger acid.
The conjugate base is formed by the removal of a proton (H⁺), which leaves a lone pair of electrons and a negative charge on the carbon atom.
For molecule (1), benzene, removal of a proton yields the phenyl anion. The negative charge is in an sp² hybridized orbital and is orthogonal to the π system. It does not participate in resonance stabilization and is highly localized, making it very unstable.
For molecule (2), removal of a proton from one of the allylic/benzylic positions gives an anion. The negative charge can be delocalized over the adjacent double bond and the benzene ring.
For molecule (3), indene, the most acidic protons are at the CH₂ group of the five-membered ring. Removal of a proton from this position produces the indenyl anion. The resulting lone pair participates in the π system. The anion has a continuous system of 10 π electrons (6 from the benzene ring, 2 from the double bond in the five-membered ring, and 2 from the lone pair). This system follows Hückel’s rule (4n+2 π electrons with n=2) for aromaticity. Because the conjugate base is aromatic, it is exceptionally stable, making indene significantly more acidic than typical hydrocarbons.
For molecule (4), removal of a proton would give an anion that can be resonance stabilized, but the resulting system is not fully conjugated or aromatic in the same continuous manner as the indenyl anion.
Therefore, the exceptionally high stability of the aromatic indenyl anion makes indene, molecule (3), the strongest acid among the given options. !

t:
Find out total number of compounds which are more stable in its ionic form
[[img:43aa75ee095c]]
s:
The stability of the ionic form of these compounds depends on whether the resulting ions are aromatic. A planar, cyclic, completely conjugated system with 4n+2 π electrons is aromatic and highly stable, while one with 4n π electrons is antiaromatic and unstable.
For compound (1), polarization of the C=O bond creates a positive charge on the five-membered ring. This gives a system with 4 π electrons, which is antiaromatic and unstable.
For compound (2), polarization of the C=O bond creates a positive charge on the three-membered ring. This gives a system with 2 π electrons, which is aromatic and stable in its ionic form.
For compound (3), polarization of the C=O bond creates a positive charge on the seven-membered ring. This gives a system with 6 π electrons, which is aromatic and stable.
For compound (4), polarization of the C=C double bond between the rings gives one ring with a positive charge (2 π electrons, aromatic) and one with a negative charge (4 π electrons, antiaromatic). The presence of the antiaromatic ring makes it unstable.
For compound (5), polarization of the C=C double bond towards the five-membered ring produces a three-membered ring with a positive charge (2 π electrons, aromatic) and a five-membered ring with a negative charge (6 π electrons, aromatic). Since both rings become aromatic, it is highly stable in its ionic form.
For compound (6), polarization of the π electrons towards the five-membered ring yields a seven-membered ring with a positive charge (6 π electrons, aromatic) and a five-membered ring with a negative charge (6 π electrons, aromatic). Both rings become aromatic, making its ionic form highly stable.
Compounds (2), (3), (5), and (6) are more stable in their ionic forms. The total number of such compounds is 4.

t: The purification of naphthalene can be done by
s:
Sublimation is a purification technique used for substances that transition directly from the solid to the vapor phase upon heating, without melting into a liquid. Naphthalene is a sublimable compound with high vapor pressure, so it easily vaporizes and deposits as pure crystals on a cooler surface, leaving non-volatile impurities behind. 

Filtration is incorrect because it is used to separate insoluble solids from liquids, not to purify solid mixtures. Evaporation and crystallization are primarily used to recover solutes dissolved in solvents, making them less direct and inefficient compared to sublimation for volatile solids.

Correct Answer: (B) sublimation

t: Chromatography is based on the phenomenon of
s:
Correct Answer: (A) adsorption

Concept:
Chromatography is an analytical separation technique based on the differential adsorption of various components of a mixture on an adsorbent (stationary phase). As the mobile phase travels over the stationary phase, substances that are adsorbed more strongly move slower, while weakly adsorbed substances move faster, leading to effective separation.

Why other options are incorrect:
- (B) Absorption is a bulk phenomenon where a substance penetrates the entire volume of a material, unlike the surface action in chromatography.
- (C) Solubility plays a role in partition, but classic chromatographic separation fundamentally depends on surface adsorption phenomena.
- (D) Chemisorption involves irreversible chemical bond formation, which would permanently trap components instead of allowing them to elute.

t:
The decreasing order of −I effect of the following is:
[ I. COOH II. F III. OR IV. NH₂ V. OH VI. Ph- ]
s:
−I effect depends on electronegativity and ability to withdraw electron density through σ-bonds.
−F (II): Most electronegative element ⇒ strongest −I effect.
−COOH (I): sp² carbon bonded to two electronegative oxygens ⇒ very strong −I effect, second to −F.
−OR (III) vs −OH (V): Both oxygen-containing; experimental data shows −OR has slightly stronger −I effect than −OH.
−NH₂ (IV): Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen ⇒ weaker −I than −OR and −OH.
−Ph (VI): sp² carbons withdraw electrons weakly ⇒ weakest −I in this list.
Final order: −F>−COOH>−OR>−OH>−NH₂>−Ph
⇒ II > I > III > V > IV > VI
Correct option: (4) .

t: Amongst the following, the total number of compounds which do not give Lassaigne’s test for nitrogen is: I. Aniline II. H₂ N−CH₂−COOH III. NH₂−NH₂ IV. Ph−N₂⁺Cl⁻ V. NH₂OH VI. NH₂−CO−NH₂ VII. Ph−NH−CO−Ph VIII. PhNO₂ IX. CH₃CHO X. CH₃CN XI. Pyridine
s:
Lassaigne’s test for nitrogen involves fusing the organic compound with sodium metal. For a positive test, the compound must contain both carbon and nitrogen to form sodium cyanide (NaCN) according to the general reaction Na+C+N→NaCN. The NaCN then reacts to form the characteristic Prussian blue complex.
The test will be negative if the compound lacks carbon, lacks nitrogen, or if it loses nitrogen gas (N₂) upon heating before the fusion reaction with sodium can take place.
Analyzing the given compounds:
Compound III (NH₂−NH₂) and Compound V (NH₂OH) contain nitrogen but do not contain carbon. They cannot form NaCN upon fusion with sodium and hence do not give Lassaigne’s test.
Compound IV (Ph−N₂⁺Cl⁻) is a diazonium salt. Upon heating during the fusion process, it readily decomposes to release N₂ gas before it can react with sodium to form NaCN. Thus, it does not give the test.
Compound IX (CH₃CHO) does not contain nitrogen, so it naturally will not give a positive test for nitrogen.
The remaining compounds (I, II, VI, VII, VIII, X, XI) contain both carbon and nitrogen in forms that can successfully fuse with sodium to produce NaCN, thus giving a positive test.
Therefore, the total number of compounds that do not give Lassaigne’s test for nitrogen is 4.

Among the following, the number of aromatic compoud(s) is:
[[img:c4aca80fe620]]
[[img:a19048ada29d]]
[[img:595c4a71d67e]]
[[img:b663e2866013]]

s:
For a compound to be aromatic, it must be cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and have (4n+2) π electrons according to Hückel’s rule.
Cyclooctatetraene has 8 π electrons. It adopts a non-planar tub shape to avoid antiaromaticity and is non-aromatic.
Cyclopropenyl anion has 4 π electrons (2 from the double bond and 2 from the negative charge) in a continuous cyclic array. It has 4n π electrons and is antiaromatic.
Cyclopropenyl cation is cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated with 2 π electrons. It satisfies Hückel’s rule for n=0 and is aromatic.
1,3-cyclohexadiene contains sp³ hybridized carbon atoms that break the cyclic conjugation. It is non-aromatic.
Cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium ion) is cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated with 6 π electrons. It satisfies Hückel’s rule for n=1 and is aromatic.
Cyclopentadienyl cation is cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated with 4 π electrons. It has 4n π electrons and is antiaromatic.
Cyclopentadienyl anion is cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated with 6 π electrons (4 from two double bonds and 2 from the negative charge). It is aromatic.
1,2-dihydronaphthalene contains an intact benzene ring which is a 6 π electron aromatic system. Because of the presence of this benzenoid ring, the compound is aromatic.
Phenanthrene is a fused polycyclic system. It is planar and fully conjugated with 14 π electrons (4n+2 for n=3). It is aromatic.
The aromatic compounds are (C), (E), (G), (H), and (I). The total number of aromatic compounds is 5.
